extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of architecture, art historians, and educated readers interested in Christian/Gothic ecclesiastical architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and prescriptive remarks for designing and judging early Christian and Romanesque church architecture, ornamentation, and furnishing (pulpits, capitals, mosaics), with emphasis on symbolic meaning and liturgical function. Targets both aesthetic/formal qualities and moral/spiritual expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of Christian architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian architecture ought to express the spiritual condition of Christians — a state of homelessness on earth, except insofar as they make the Most High their habitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general character (the building's overall spiritual expression) is more important than separate architectural details; the architect should design to embody and communicate this inward spiritual condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basilica plan and interior arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The church should be built on the Basilica plan: body divided into nave and aisles by rows of massive shafts, nave raised above aisles and pierced with arched windows; nave breadth significantly greater than aisles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interior arrangement must be clear and functional; proportions (e.g., nave nearly twice the breadth of aisles at Torcello) and placement of windows contribute to light and the intended effect of the interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and variety in capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals should not be mere indifferent imitations of classical orders but show distinct and varied designs, each carefully worked to produce calculated effects from every chisel touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value imaginative variation (different designs for each capital), strong chisel work (sharp, deep penetrations), and individualized treatment rather than repetitive copying of Corinthian forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative transformation of classical motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical motifs (e.g., the Corinthian acanthus) should be transformed imaginatively rather than copied; stems may be boldly detached, leaves placed in unconventional positions, or classical fillets turned into living serpentine forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such transformations convey life and Gothic energy; specific treatment (rounded lobes, trefoiled leaves, deep drill holes) enhances shadow, perspective, and expressive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic meaning in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament should carry Christian symbolic meanings (e.g., vine as a symbol of Christ; serpent as sign of eternity of dominion or Satan subdued).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptural elements should be intelligible as symbols to reinforce theological themes and the worshippers' devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminousness and use of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Churches should admit and diffuse sunlight freely; luminousness is preferable to gloom for expressing hope and comfort in Christian worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive gloom and dark colors in decoration; design windows, walls, and spatial proportions so that even fine sculptural and mosaic detail remains visible in twilight, fostering a hopeful, not terrifying, devotional atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of iconographic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of subjects for mosaics and imagery should focus on the central spiritual facts (e.g., Christ's present mercy and His coming judgment) rather than worldly, political, satirical, or trivial scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concentrated, earnest iconography demonstrates singleness of faith; avoid mixed or profane subject-matter that distracts worshippers from core religious truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and tonal restraint in sacred imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mosaics and frescoes in early Christian churches should use fair and bright colors rather than dark, artificial shadows or sombre palettes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bright coloring aligns with the builders' hopefulness and avoids instilling terror; painting choices should reinforce the intended devotional mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workmanship suited to place
rubrics_metrics.description: Carving and ornamentation should be executed with finish and beauty appropriate to the place they occupy; pieces carved specifically for the church are preferable to repurposed fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, elements should be made for their site; the best and most beautiful work belongs where it is intended to be seen and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture as surface enrichment vs narrative legibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In early Romanesque work, large sculptured surfaces often serve enrichment rather than being expected to present a traceable narrative chain of thought to the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrichment of surface is legitimate: sculptural patterns may be treated like lace or embroidery, to be applied and cut as needed; absence of narrative legibility is not always a defect but can indicate vitality and practical design priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careless fitting of ornament as evidence of vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Rough or careless fitting of repurposed ornament may indicate the energy and fertility of a school of builders rather than mere bluntness or savageness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret such treatments contextually: if the new work equals or surpasses the old in execution, rough reuse suggests confidence and an ability to create replacements easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit scale: simplicity over splendour
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulpits ought never to be highly decorated or colossal in scale; excessive magnificence can make the preacher appear mean or diminish the efficacy of preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler forms that do not overshadow the speaker; overly magnificent pulpits often lead preachers to use temporary platforms elsewhere, reducing liturgical coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit ornament: chaste, grave, noble
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ornament admitted on a pulpit should be chaste, grave, and noble in kind, honoring God's word rather than showcasing human learning or ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decoration should support the pulpit's role as the seat of a divine message, not as a stage for rhetorical display; avoid ornament of oratory in the messenger's mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit form and functional design for preaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The pulpit's form should afford the preacher full room for the action of the entire person, provide practical features (e.g., a hollowed desk that holds a book without slipping), and present a severe simplicity that aids impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design details (slightly oval shape, central bracket, ledges to steady books, minimal decorative elements) enhance the preacher's ability to address and move an audience effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Furniture priorities: honor the Word over comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Church furniture should be designed more to honor God's word than solely to provide ease to the preacher; austerity can convey dignity and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept some austerity (e.g., uncomfortably simple raised seats of marble, arms as distinction rather than convenience) when it reinforces the spiritual and disciplinary aims of the liturgical setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural symbolism relative to context
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural elements and their placement should reinforce communal and cultural symbols (e.g., the Church as a ship, the bishop as pilot), which heighten meaning for worshippers who inhabit that world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use site-specific symbolic resonances (sea, isolation, refuge) so that occupants can readily imagine and feel the intended spiritual analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions, shafts, and diffusion of light to avoid oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Large shafts, frank diffusion of light, and delicate carving prevent architectural severity from becoming oppressive and allow detail to be appreciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance mass and light: choose shaft proportions, window placement, and carving depth to produce graceful lines and visible ornament without oppressive darkness.
